title: Environmental Science
summary: Learn how natural systems work and how people affect them: ecosystems and energy flow, nutrient and water cycles, biodiversity and conservation, pollution and waste, natural resources and land use, and sustainability and environmental management.
audience: Students, teachers, community leaders and anyone who cares about the environment

body.p: Environmental science studies how natural systems work and how human activity affects them, drawing on biology, chemistry, geography and economics. An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and their physical environment, such as a forest, wetland, savanna or coral reef.

list: Producers (plants, algae) capture sunlight through photosynthesis.
Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers; secondary and tertiary consumers eat other animals.
Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.
Food webs show the many linked feeding relationships in an ecosystem.

body.p: Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next; the rest is used for life processes or lost as heat. If producers capture 10 000 kJ, herbivores get about 1000 kJ, the next level about 100 kJ and top predators about 10 kJ. This is why there are far fewer lions than zebras, and why eating lower on the food chain uses less land.

body.tip: Draw a food web for a habitat near you and predict what happens if one species disappears.

body.p: Matter cycles through ecosystems, unlike energy, which flows through and is lost as heat.

list: Water cycle: evaporation from oceans and lakes, transpiration from plants, condensation into clouds, precipitation, and run-off and infiltration into groundwater. Forests help recycle rainfall inland.

Carbon cycle: plants take in CO₂ in photosynthesis; respiration, decomposition and burning return it. Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests add extra carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, driving climate change.

Nitrogen cycle: nitrogen-fixing bacteria (some in legume roots) turn atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants use; decomposers and other bacteria recycle it. Excess fertiliser washing into rivers causes algal blooms (eutrophication) that starve water of oxygen.

body.p: Human activity changes these cycles at global scale, with effects on climate, water supplies and food production.

body.tip: Trace one carbon atom from the air into a maize plant, a person and back to the air; it makes the cycle concrete.

body.p: Biodiversity is the variety of life: genetic diversity within species, the diversity of species, and the diversity of ecosystems. Africa holds remarkable biodiversity, from the Congo Basin rainforest to the Cape Floral Region and East African savannas.

list: Ecosystem services: pollination of crops, clean water, fertile soil, flood control and climate regulation.
Food, medicines and materials.
Tourism and livelihoods.
Cultural and spiritual value, and the right of species to exist.
Threats: habitat loss, overexploitation (including poaching and overfishing), invasive species, pollution and climate change.
Protected areas and community conservancies, where local people benefit from wildlife.
Restoring degraded land and wetlands.
Keystone species, such as elephants that shape savanna vegetation, have outsized effects; protecting them protects many other species.
International agreements such as the Convention on Biological Diversity and CITES (on wildlife trade).

body.tip: Conservation succeeds best when local communities share in its benefits and decisions.

body.p: Sources include vehicles, industry, burning waste and cooking with wood, charcoal or kerosene indoors. Fine particles damage lungs and hearts; indoor smoke is a major health risk, especially for women and children. Cleaner fuels and stoves, better vehicles and controlling open burning reduce it.

list: Sewage and poor sanitation spread diseases such as cholera.
Fertiliser and manure run-off cause eutrophication.
Industrial and mining waste can add toxic metals such as mercury and lead.
Plastic waste blocks drains, causing floods, and harms marine life.

body.p: The waste hierarchy ranks options: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, and dispose safely as the last resort. If a household throws away 0.5 kg of plastic a day, that is 182.5 kg a year, or 730 kg for four such households; reducing single-use plastic and recycling make a real difference. Informal waste pickers recover large amounts of recyclable material in many African cities.

body.tip: Audit your household waste for a week, then pick one change, such as reusable bags, and stick to it.

body.p: Renewable resources (forests, fish, water, soil) can regenerate if not overused; non-renewable resources (fossil fuels, minerals) are finite.

Forests are cleared for farming, charcoal, timber and settlements. If a forest of 50 000 km² loses 2% a year, the first year's loss is 1000 km², and after 10 years about 40 854 km² remain. Land degradation and desertification reduce soil fertility and food security. Responses include agroforestry, the Great Green Wall initiative across the Sahel, community forest management and efficient cookstoves that use less charcoal.

list: Many regions face water stress; efficient irrigation, rainwater harvesting and protecting catchments help.
Mining brings revenue and jobs but can cause pollution, land damage and conflict; environmental rules, rehabilitation and fair benefit-sharing are essential.
Overfishing threatens coastal livelihoods; quotas and marine protected areas help stocks recover.

body.tip: Use compound-decline calculations to see how small yearly losses add up over decades.

body.p: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. It balances environmental, social and economic goals.

list: Environmental impact assessment (EIA): a process, required by law in many countries, to predict and reduce the environmental effects of projects such as roads, dams and mines before approval.
Renewable energy, such as solar, wind and hydro, reduces pollution and greenhouse emissions.
Circular economy: design products to be reused, repaired and recycled instead of discarded.
Environmental laws and agencies set standards for emissions, waste and land use.
Citizen action: tree planting, clean-ups, monitoring pollution and holding polluters accountable.

body.p: The UN Sustainable Development Goals include goals on clean water, clean energy, climate action, life below water and life on land, linking the environment to health, jobs and equality.

body.tip: Ask of any project: who benefits, who bears the costs, and what will the environment look like in 30 years?
